title_en: Why I Still Buy Paper Books
title_ru: Почему я всё ещё покупаю бумажные книги
description_ru: Автор объясняет, почему любит бумажные книги, хотя пользуется и электронной: память, отвлекающие факторы, книжные магазины и компромисс.
text:
I own an e-reader, and I like it. It is light, it holds hundreds of books, and I can read on it in bed without a lamp. I bought it for a long holiday two years ago, and I used it every day. Nevertheless, when I get home, I still go to the bookshop and buy paper books. Many of my friends find this strange. "It is the twenty-first century," they say. "Why do you carry such heavy things?" In this essay, I want to explain why I believe that paper books are still worth the trouble.

The first reason is that paper is simply nicer to read. I know that this sounds old-fashioned, but science partly agrees with me. Several studies have found that people who read on paper often remember more of the story than people who read the same text on a screen. One idea is that a physical book gives your brain more clues. You know that an important event happened on the left page, about a third of the way through, and you can see how much is still to come. On a screen, every page looks the same, and the text seems to slide away.

Another reason is that screens are distracting. When I read on my tablet, I am only one touch away from messages, news and videos. I have lost count of the times that I opened an e-book and ended up checking the weather instead. A paper book cannot send me a notification. It does not need charging, and it works on a plane, on a beach or during a power cut. If I drop it in the bath, I will be annoyed, but I will not need to buy a new one.

Books are also objects that you can share, and I think that is important. I have lent novels to friends, borrowed some from my grandmother, and found notes written in the margins of second-hand copies. Once, I discovered a pressed flower inside an old edition of a poetry collection, and I wondered for days who had left it there. You cannot lend an e-book so easily, and you certainly cannot find a mysterious flower in one. A shelf full of books also tells a story about a person. When I visit someone's home, I always look at the books first.

Reading in print has one more advantage for me: it slows me down. I turn the pages, I notice the cover, and I am less tempted to hurry to the end. Finally, I think that the shops matter. If everybody switched to e-books, bookshops would close, and our towns would lose some of their personality. A small bookshop is a place where you can talk to someone who knows what you might enjoy, where you can discover an author that you have never heard of, and where you can spend an hour without being asked to buy anything. Online shops are efficient, but their suggestions are based on what you have already bought, so they rarely surprise you.

Of course, I do not want to be unfair to e-books. They have several real advantages. For people with poor eyesight, they allow the type to be made bigger. Students can carry a whole library instead of a heavy bag. Readers in remote areas, or in countries without good bookshops, can download almost anything in seconds. E-books are often cheaper, and they use less paper, which is better for forests. If you travel often, they are a wonderful invention. I would not give up my e-reader, and I think it would be silly to claim that one type of book is perfect for all situations.

I also notice that the two formats are not really enemies. When e-books first appeared, many people predicted that printed books would disappear within a few years. That has not happened. Sales of paper books have remained surprisingly stable, and in some countries they have even grown. It seems that many readers, like me, enjoy using both: an e-reader for travelling and a real book for the sofa.

So my advice is simple. If you have only ever read on a screen, try a paper book for a month and see whether you notice a difference. If you read mainly on paper, consider an e-reader for your next trip. Either way, the most important thing is to read, and to enjoy it. As long as people keep turning pages, whether real or virtual, stories will survive. Personally, though, I will keep buying paper books, and I will keep complaining about the weight of my suitcase.

questions.question: Why do studies suggest that paper is better for remembering?
questions.answer: A physical book gives the brain more clues, such as where an event happened in the book.

questions.question: Why are screens distracting?
questions.answer: They are one touch away from messages, news and videos.

questions.question: What does the author like about bookshops?
questions.answer: You can talk to someone who knows books and discover new authors.

questions.question: What is the author's advice at the end?
questions.answer: Try both formats; the important thing is to read.
